newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's security council wants fair polls.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's security council wants fair polls.

text.p: Pakistan's newly-formed and controversial Defence and National Security Council told the caretaker government on Wednesday to ensure free and fair elections on February 3.

An official statement after a seven-hour first meeting of the council of politicians and and military men praised the caretakers for arresting "a downslide of the economy" and urged the implementation of an anti-corruption accountability process.

The widely-criticised body met two days after President Farooq Leghari formed it amid uncertainty about elections boycotted by three small groups and after ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto said she would not accept the results if the vote was held under the present set-up established by her opponents.
"The council was of the view that it was the constitutional duty of the government to ensure the holding of free, fair and impartial elections...," the official statement said.
"The council was of the view that the process of accoutability must be expedited...."
A second Islamic religious party, Jamiat Ulema-i-Pakistan, said on Wednesday it would boycott the vote because its demand for a system of proportional representation had not been met.
The decision was announced in the southern port city of Karachi as the main fundamentalist Islamist Jamaat-i-Islami party held another anti-election protest sit-in there.
A third, smaller group, Tehrik-i-Istiqlal of former air force chief Asghar Khan, has also announced a poll boycott.
The Council for Defence and National Security, grouping military chiefs and ministers, has drawn widespread criticism.

Leghari has taken a central role in Pakistani politics since he dissolved the National Assembly (lower house) on November 5 and sacked prime minister Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old government on allegations of corruption and misrule.
His latest action has generated a fierce row over whether he and the caretaker government have overstepped their powers.

The government seemed isolated in a Senate (upper house of parliament) debate on the issue on Wednesday. Six of seven senators who spoke blasted the council, leaving only the seventh, a government minister, to defend its formation.
The government says the council can give only non-binding advice and its creation has not violated the constitution.
But Bhutto and other critics have accused Leghari of trying to drag the armed forces into politics and acting beyond his constitutional powers in forming the new body.

Its military members are the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff committee and the chiefs of the army, navy and air force. It includes the president as chairman, the prime minister and ministers of defence, foreign affairs, interior and finance.

The council is empowered to advise on defence and national security issues and on economic and financial policies affecting them. It can also make recommendations on internal security matters and the proclamation of an emergency.
The president may refer any issue to the council without consulting the prime minister.

In other developments, former cricket hero and aspiring politician Imran Khan fended off questions on Wednesday about the source of his election war-chest and allegations that he was the father of an illegitimate child.

"If anyone proves that I have taken even one paisa (one hundredth of a rupee) from the Jewish lobby, I am ready to leave politics and go to jail," he told reporters before kicking off his election campaign with a rally in Karachi.
Imran married Jemima Goldsmith, the daughter of wealthy Anglo-French financier Sir James Goldsmith, who is Jewish, in 1995. Jemima, a convert to Islam, gave birth to a son last year.
He has been bombarded with queries about Sita White, a former girlfriend who filed a paternity suit in Los Angeles on Monday seeking to prove Imran fathered her four-year-old daughter.
